summary: Describes how endpoints can negotiate the ability to send arbitrary values in the second-most significant bit of QUIC packets. Doing so helps prevent middleboxes from depending on the bit's value, keeping the protocol flexible for future changes. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: If everyone always sets a switch to on, someone will build a machine that breaks when it is off. This lets the switch flip randomly so nobody can rely on it.

questions: what does greasing the quic bit mean
what is the grease_quic_bit transport parameter
subtitle: A QUIC extension that lets endpoints scramble one fixed header bit so networks cannot come to depend on it.

tldr.problem: The second-most significant bit of the first byte of every QUIC version 1 packet has a fixed value. If networks start relying on it, nobody will be able to give that bit a meaning later.
tldr.mechanism: Endpoints advertise an empty grease_quic_bit transport parameter (0x2ab2). A peer that sees it may then set the QUIC Bit to an unpredictable value, and the advertiser MUST accept packets where it is 0.
tldr.outcome: The bit stays free for future extensions, at the cost of making QUIC harder to identify for network operators who classify traffic without endpoint cooperation.

today: RFC 9287 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the QUIC Bit Needs Protecting
sections.content:
The version-independent definition of QUIC (RFC 8999) deliberately describes only a very narrow set of fields that anyone other than the endpoints can see. Beyond those invariant characteristics, very little of QUIC's "wire image" (RFC 8546) is visible.

In QUIC version 1 (RFC 9000), the second-most significant bit of the first byte of every packet has a fixed value. The point of the fixed value is to let endpoints efficiently tell QUIC apart from other protocols. Because it can identify a packet as QUIC, it is sometimes called the QUIC Bit.

The RFC argues that where endpoints and their intermediaries do not need the fixed value, sending the same value in every packet is more of a liability than an asset. If systems come to depend on it, it might become infeasible to define a QUIC version that gives the bit a meaning.
sections.eli5: One tiny switch on every QUIC message is always set the same way. If people start counting on that, nobody can ever use the switch for something new.

sections.title: The Grease QUIC Bit Transport Parameter
sections.content:
The extension defines the grease_quic_bit transport parameter, with value 0x2ab2, for QUIC version 1. Both client and server can send it. It is sent with an empty value, and an endpoint that understands it MUST treat a non-empty value as a connection error of type TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR.

An endpoint that advertises the parameter MUST accept packets with the QUIC Bit set to 0. The QUIC Bit is the second-most significant bit of the first byte, that is, the value 0x40.

In other words, sending the parameter is a promise: "I do not depend on this bit, so you can put anything in it." The hope stated in the RFC is that by sending different values the bit will remain available for future use.
sections.eli5: Each side says "I will not be upset if that switch is off." Only after hearing that is the other side allowed to flip it.

sections.title: Clearing the QUIC Bit
sections.content:
An endpoint that receives the parameter from its peer SHOULD set the QUIC Bit to an unpredictable value, unless another extension assigns the bit a specific meaning. Once an endpoint has received and processed the peer's transport parameters, it can set the bit to 0 on all packets it sends, which could include Initial, Handshake and Retry packets.

A client MAY also set the bit to 0 in Initial, Handshake or 0-RTT packets sent before it has the server's transport parameters. It MUST NOT do so unless its Initial packets carry a token from the server's NEW_TOKEN frame, received less than 604800 seconds (7 days) earlier on a connection where the server also included the parameter. The RFC says this limit allows for changes in server configuration: if a server stops supporting the extension and the client does not set the bit, the server might drop packets and the connection fails.

A server MUST set the bit to 0 only after processing the client's transport parameters. A server MUST NOT remember from a previous connection that a client negotiated the extension. In general, an endpoint MUST NOT set the bit to 0 without knowing the peer supports the extension. Stateless Reset packets are only used after connection state is lost, so endpoints are unlikely to be able to clear the bit on them.
sections.eli5: You may only flip the switch once you are sure the other side said it is fine. Servers must ask again each time and cannot just remember from last time.

sections.title: Using the QUIC Bit for Something Else
sections.content:
The purpose of the extension is to let later extensions use the QUIC Bit. An extension that gives the bit a meaning can be negotiated at the same time as grease_quic_bit. The recipient then has to be able to tell a randomized value from one that carries information. Extensions that use the bit MUST negotiate their use before acting on any semantic.

For example, an extension might define its own transport parameter alongside grease_quic_bit. The bit might be set by the extension's rules, or it might be randomized. To avoid acting on a randomized signal, the extension can require endpoints to set the bit by its rules but defer acting on it until the extension's transport parameter has been received.

Such an extension can also be negotiated without grease_quic_bit, but including both lets the bit be greased even when the alternative use is not supported.
sections.eli5: If someone invents a real job for the switch, both sides first agree to it. Until then, a flip might just be random, so you do not act on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security considerations for endpoints or for entities that can rely on endpoint cooperation. However, the change makes it more difficult to identify QUIC without the endpoints' cooperation.

That sometimes works against the security goals of network operators who rely on network classification to identify threats. The RFC points to a draft on the manageability of QUIC for a fuller treatment.
sections.eli5: Hiding the always-the-same switch makes it harder for network guards to spot QUIC traffic by looking at it, and some guards do not like that.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC registers the grease_quic_bit transport parameter in the "QUIC Transport Parameters" registry. The registration has value 0x2ab2, status Permanent, specification RFC 9287 and date 2022-07-13. The change controller is the IETF and the contact is the QUIC Working Group.
sections.eli5: The number 0x2ab2 is officially written down in a list so nobody else uses it for something different.
